I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea. No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea. Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it. For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others. I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same. To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans. # Inside the Cottage Industry That is The AI Training Data Market

Frontier AI labs are spending billions on training data. An army of brokers, data sellers, and self-proclaimed insiders wants a cut. Behind the seven-figure promises is a far stranger, messier business than social media would have you believe.

Spend five minutes on X, and you might conclude that selling AI training data is the easiest way to become a millionaire in 2026. Every other week, another self-proclaimed data broker announces a direct pipeline to frontier labs. Someone has discovered that your company's Slack messages could be worth millions. A new startup claims to have cracked the market with proprietary sourcing technology, exclusive relationships, or some mysterious data-quality advantage.

The landing pages are remarkably similar. Seven-figure payouts, urgent calls for enterprise data, and promises to unlock the hidden value of information your business already generates. Apparently, all you need is a company with a few years of operational history and a middleman who knows someone at OpenAI or Anthropic.

The reality is considerably less glamorous. Many of these businesses are glorified referral operations. Others are labor marketplaces, data resellers, or small research shops packaging synthetic examples that increasingly capable AI models can generate themselves. Their supposedly proprietary technology often boils down to publicly available models, a few scripts, and some quality checks. The claims of privileged relationships are difficult to verify, as are the extraordinary payouts advertised to prospective sellers.

Yet dismissing the entire industry as another AI gold rush would be a mistake. The money is very real. The barriers to entry are often surprisingly low. And the distance between those two facts explains much of the absurdity playing out on X.

Consider what happened to Spirit Airlines.

In May 2026, the American budget airline ceased operations. Three months later, Google won an auction for something the bankrupt company had left behind: its internal business data. The price was $10 million. The proposed purchase included years of employee communications, spreadsheets, calendars, and operational records. Mercor, an AI data company, submitted the $7.5 million alternate bid. Google wanted the information for product development and AI training.

The transaction attracted objections from labor unions and more than 120 American lawmakers concerned about employee privacy. After Google agreed to additional protections, including stronger de-identification and exclusions for sensitive records, a federal bankruptcy judge approved the deal on November 17 .

Think about what just happened. An airline went out of business, but its digital history was worth $10 million to a company building AI. Those records weren't originally created to train a language model. They existed because employees had spent years answering emails, coordinating schedules, resolving problems, and keeping an airline operating. For an AI developer, that history potentially contains something the public internet rarely offers: an account of how work actually gets done inside a business.

It's a compelling example of why enterprise data can be valuable. It is also an extraordinarily unusual transaction that shouldn't be mistaken for a typical corporate data sale. Most businesses do not have bidders lining up at bankruptcy auctions. A prospective seller with ten years of Slack messages is far more likely to encounter a long qualification process, uncertain demand, privacy complications, and a broker who cannot actually get the deal done.

To understand why this market is attracting so many hopeful entrepreneurs, we need to follow the money.

### The Other Billion-Dollar AI Business

In July 2026, The Information reported that Mercor had surpassed $2 billion in gross annualized revenue. Handshake AI, another company supplying expert-generated training data, had reportedly reached a $1 billion gross annualized run rate earlier that year. Surge AI and Scale AI had also reached billion-dollar revenue or gross-sales levels in recent years.

These are remarkable numbers for companies whose activities include recruiting people, preparing training examples, evaluating model outputs, and delivering datasets to AI developers. The spending also shows up in the buyers' financial disclosures.

In its November 2026 securities filing , Anthropic reported that external vendor costs related to data quality and performance evaluations increased by $757 million during the first nine months of 2026 , compared with the same period a year earlier. That's the increase, not the total amount spent. The category includes evaluation and data-quality services rather than just licensing existing corporate records. Even with those qualifications, the scale is extraordinary.

Why are the world's most sophisticated AI laboratories spending so much on information when their own models can already generate seemingly unlimited amounts of text, code, and synthetic examples?

The answer is that generating plausible information isn't the same as producing a useful learning signal. An AI model can read every accounting textbook ever published and still struggle to reconcile an unfamiliar company's books. It can generate thousands of lines of code without reliably fixing a bug in a complicated production system.

Pre-training teaches models patterns, language, and broad knowledge. Post-training uses demonstrations, feedback, and reinforcement learning to improve how they perform tasks. A model might know the definition of a financial reconciliation. Learning to complete one requires understanding which records to inspect, how discrepancies arise, what constitutes a valid adjustment, and when the books actually balance. The same applies to software engineering, legal analysis, scientific research, and countless other professional activities.

This creates demand for examples of real work, including the decisions, mistakes, corrections, and outcomes that accompany it.

The people getting paid to teach AI their jobs

Consider Jessica Crutcher, an American arbitrator who spends her spare time creating complicated legal problems for AI models. As Business Insider reported , she works through Mercor, devising disputes that require sophisticated legal reasoning. Other participating lawyers create difficult scenarios, review AI-generated answers, and explain why particular responses are wrong. Companies have advertised rates as high as $200 an hour for some legal experts.

The value isn't necessarily in having a lawyer type out an answer. It's in finding problems sophisticated AI models still struggle to solve, then establishing what a correct solution looks like.

In Shenzhen, an architect using the pseudonym Cuicui has a very different motivation. Her earnings from architecture had fallen sharply during China's construction slowdown. As Rest of World reported , she began spending evenings teaching AI models how to prepare building proposals and conduct profitability analyses, drawing on her actual professional work. The extra income helped pay her mortgage and her child's expenses.

There's an uncomfortable irony here. Professionals worried about their economic futures are being paid to transfer aspects of their expertise into machines that may eventually perform some of their work. The arrangement is perfectly rational for everyone involved. The labs need realistic professional knowledge, vendors need contributors, and professionals need income. The longer-term consequences are considerably less clear.

And expert labor represents only one corner of this industry.

### Your Company's Digital Exhaust Is Someone Else's Training Data

A second category of suppliers doesn't create new training data at all. It licenses information generated through ordinary business operations.

Think about what a company accumulates over a decade: customer support tickets, sales conversations, engineering documentation, pull requests, financial reconciliations, internal communications, contracts, approvals, incident reports, and performance reviews. Most of this information was never intended for AI development. It exists because organizations need records to function.

But those archives can reveal patterns of professional activity that are difficult to reproduce from public information. A source-code repository is useful. A repository connected to bug reports, engineering discussions, attempted fixes, failed tests, and final resolutions may be substantially more useful for training a coding agent.

An invoice is a piece of information. The entire process through which an accountant investigates a discrepancy, requests supporting documents, makes an adjustment, and receives approval is an example of a workflow. That distinction matters because the training signal often lies in the relationships between records, rather than the records themselves.

Data acquisition companies have noticed. Micro1 currently advertises payments ranging from $100,000 to more than $3 million for qualifying enterprise operational datasets. Its website identifies software engineering, finance, customer support, sales, legal work, and logistics among the potentially relevant domains.

It's a brilliant acquisition pitch. Years of mundane operational records are suddenly being presented as an asset that could generate a substantial windfall. But an advertised payout range is not a market-clearing price. The company still needs to qualify, establish what information it can legally license, demonstrate usefulness, and complete a transaction. There is no reason to assume every enterprise dataset will attract a buyer, let alone a seven-figure offer.

The numbers make much more sense when understood as the upper end of a highly selective market rather than an ordinary price for corporate records.

A different example comes from healthcare. In October 2026, Tempus AI disclosed agreements worth up to $192.5 million over approximately five years with Bristol Myers Squibb and Pathos AI. One agreement involved supplying up to 500,000 de-identified neurology patient records at $100 per delivered record, with additional compensation for updates.

These were specialized pharmaceutical data and software arrangements, not conventional purchases of general-purpose LLM training datasets. Nevertheless, they illustrate how valuable structured, rights-cleared information can become when it addresses a specific research need.

The common thread is that the data has to solve a problem somebody is willing to pay for. That last part gets lost in much of the social-media excitement.

### Meet the Middlemen

The cottage-industry character of this market becomes obvious once you examine the businesses connecting suppliers to AI developers.

At one end are referral agents. Their operation can be remarkably simple: identify a company that might have useful data, introduce it to a buyer or established vendor, and collect a fee if the introduction produces a qualifying transaction. Micro1, for instance, has publicly advertised a $50,000 referral reward for introducing eligible enterprises under specified program conditions. That creates an incentive for anyone with corporate contacts to become a data sourcer.

At the next level are brokers, who may represent data owners, find qualified buyers, negotiate licensing terms, and coordinate due diligence. Aggregators acquire rights to information from multiple sources and package those assets for onward licensing.

Then come expert workforce platforms, managed annotation providers, specialist research firms, and developers building executable environments for reinforcement learning. They all get called data companies. Their actual businesses couldn't be more different.

# I’m Glad that Lit Awards are Going to AI

It’s 2015 in the main auditorium of WorldCon. Outside the raging forest fires of the Pacific Northwest have turned the sky into a red Mordor haze. The air filters of the convention center are in overdrive as the winner of tonight’s seventh Hugo Award is about to be announced. Every breath holds for one of Science Fiction Fandom’s greatest moments of reckoning.

“The award for Best Related Work goes to…

…No Award.”

A cheer rocks the room. My voice is among them, elated. My date is silent. Then she turns her face into my shoulder and cries softly. I’m confused by her reaction, she was just as upset by the Sad Puppies vandalization as all the rest of us.

“It was all just so pointless,” she said later. “There was no good outcome. No matter what happened, we all lost.”

In 2015 the Hugo Awards, once among the most prestigious awards in Speculative Fiction 1 , had been hijacked by a coordinated group with a grudge. They’d packed the ballot with their picks (most of them quite bad). Some categories didn’t have a single nominee that hadn’t been forced on by them. After discussion the fan community converged on “it would be better to vote for No Award over any of these pretenders” as the way to deal with this. But with nearly 6000 ballots cast it was impossible to know if the word had gotten out to everyone, and if everyone was on board. Some people thought it would be better to choose among the options given than leave the award unawarded that year.

The first six awards given out in the first six categories that night all had at least one nominee that hadn’t been placed there by the Sad Puppies group. Each award was given to a non-Sad-Puppy nominee. The award for Best Related Work was the first one that didn’t have a single non-Puppy nominee to vote for. It was the test to see if our community was willing to shut out the vandals, or let them have what they wanted. When the words “No Award” rang out the floodgates of relief burst. We may not have an award this year, but at least the bastards wouldn’t have their scalp.

I had been writing about this for months in my old blog. I’d read and reviewed all the novels, short stories, and novelettes that year. I’d previously been quoted by the head instigator of the Sad Puppies group. I’d been quoted in File770, the SF community gossip magazine. I cared a lot about these awards. I put significant effort into participating in them and going to the conventions where they were awarded. I was very defensive of efforts to hurt them. This was my community. Don’t come for my friends.

That was over a decade ago. Well before AI. Recently “The Serpent in the Grove” won the Commonwealth Short Story Prize despite being entirely written by AI . This was not an AI prize, and there was a scandal. “Where Water Works” won the first Almadía Ventosa-Arrufat International Short Novel Prize and was also written by AI . The top award from the Caine Prize went to a work primarily written by AI .

This sort of degradation of literature awards would have angered me ten years ago. Perhaps broken my heart a bit, though I probably wouldn’t admit it. For such blatant slop to pollute something I cared about would’ve killed me. Now I smile every time I see it. Now I want it to keep happening, more and more, until the stink of it chokes out the very Heavens. I’m not proud of this, but I don’t apologize for it. It can only happen to those who deserve it.

## “Mother is the name for God on the lips and hearts of all children”

Let me caveat my next point — I greatly admire my father. Maybe I idolize him. He’s an incredible man who took major risks to smuggle his family out of an authoritarian hellhole (communist Poland) and bring them to a foreign country to make a new life. I owe him so much. Also, he was a man with faults like any other, he was making it up as he went along just like any of us, and he had an infant son literally two decades younger than I am right now.

I don’t think he knew that I didn’t have many friends growing up . That was fine 2 because I had books. I had a thousand worlds full of the most fantastic places and exciting people. The world around me could suck to a fair degree and I’d just slip into a better world whenever I wanted. My father didn’t have this luxury. He was navigating a world without plot armor, trying to shield me from the worst effects of growing up poor. He didn’t have time to read for pleasure. That’s what kids do, not adults.

As I grew older my love of fiction only intensified. Rather than outgrowing fiction, my tastes became more complex and (dare I say) refined. But the books still had space ships or swashbucklers on the covers. The older I got the more disdainful he became. He asked me once what I spent all my time reading, and I showed him, somewhat proudly, one of the more interesting books I was into.

“Bajki,” he said, the Polish word for children’s fairytales. He did the thing with his voice that I hated, that he’d been doing since soon after I hit puberty, which said “it’s not even worth my time to engage with you.” He asked what I was doing with these child’s stories. I told him I was going to write. I would make something like this. He let his contempt, his disappointment that this was what his son was aspiring to, show openly.

They say spite is the best motivator . My dad didn’t know about the Hugo or Nebula awards. He didn’t know there was an entire world of prestigious science fiction read by Serious People who use it to think and discourse. I knew that if I told him about it he’d dismiss them too, wouldn’t even bother looking into what was being done in speculative fiction to interrogate the world and our place within existence as fallen humans. There was no argument that a fourteen-year-old reading SF could make that he would listen to. But I did know that if I grew up and I came home with an award, or better yet, if I flew him out to the awards ceremony and made him sit there and watch as respected professionals celebrated and awarded me personally with a trophy and a title that would follow me for the rest of my life, he would be forced to say that I was right. I wanted to win the most prestigious award I could so I could rub it in his smug, stupid face. To show I was respected and deserved his respect as well. Maybe even his admiration.

## Why We Write

I don’t start writing until my 30s. Writing doesn’t really pay money, with a handful of extremely notable exceptions. People do not write for money. They write because they love to write, and they are fed by the recognition of their peers. To a first approximation it’s correct to say that authors are motivated by prestige rather than money.

By the time I started writing I’d happily established a toehold in the SF Lit world. I’m in a reading group with fellow local authors who enjoy my takes. I’m in a writers group that includes currently professional authors, has Hugo award winners as alumni, and they are impressed with many of my efforts. I helped run the Literary Track of Denver Comic Con, I had dinner with award winners. I have a group of other hopeful up-comers I’m tight with.

The literary scene has always been pretty leftist. The scifi lit scene is several degrees more leftist than that. SF lit had always prided itself on being ahead of the curve on civil rights, religious tolerance, sexual freedom, women’s lib, gay rights, etc. The scene leaned hard into wokism from the first moments it shrieked itself into existence. Which I thought was good because I was also quite left. If one award nominee slot every year went to advocacy that was fine. 3 Maybe even good.

In February of 2015 my first short story was published in Asimov’s magazine. (It was later shortlisted for the 2015 Sidewise Award). That same month K. Tempest Bradford (established editor and thought leader) pushed for everyone to stop reading white men for a year.

The official article in TIME magazine is toned down. I was in the audience when she argued for this during a panel discussion at the convention where the Hugo Awards are given out . The argument was quite direct when she spoke freely. My community erupted into discourse not about if this was an acceptable thing to propose, but about how much one should eliminate white men from the SF community. Should we stop reading them for a year, or only a few weeks? Is it OK to read those who are pre-vetted by trusted editors? Can one save the works of favorite authors to read after the embargo? Maybe we should just not read any by default, but if a piece is known to be really good and it happens to be by a white man it’s OK to read it? Didn’t white men deserve this? Couldn’t they take one measly year of no readers? We all know this won’t happen anyway, haha, so what does it say about someone if they feel threatened by it?

The fact is, white men were still being published, and read, and respected in the community. So saying “I feel this would hurt me” would be an acknowledgement that one believes that their work isn’t good enough to stand on its own. Every year some new white men get their first publishing contract in the SF world, despite being white men. Every now and then they’ll have a hit, just like anyone else. If you can’t get published, if you never make it big, well, you obviously just didn’t have the talent needed to make it. Happens to 99% of people who try. There is no way to say “this is fucked up” without being seen as another no-talent white male blaming his problems on minorities and women. All you can do is keep your head down, keep writing with everything you have, and trust that the crazies will be ignored and you’ll be treated fairly. Everyone is basically good.

We rally to rebuff the Sad Puppies as a united community, and it feels good.

## I Get The Hint

I keep writing. I get published in Analog magazine as well, and several anthologies, and win a Writers of the Future award. But it’s getting harder to be in this community. More and more works that are celebrated seem bad . It’s not random either, it’s not just very personable authors getting love from their fans/friends, as the Sad Puppies had complained about — now the badness is strongly correlated with activism. After a few years the only men left in the major awards are those who’ve led woke charges.

My favorite author, N.K. Jemisin, who I hope to some day write half as well as, weighs in strongly in favor of my demographic being removed from SF lit. This really hurts. I had idolized her.

I notice a lot of men authors are adopting They/Them pronouns. Eventually even the “ally” men are removed. The book club I was in reads the Hugo Nominated novels, short stories, and novelettes every year. More and more in the later years I was reading straight racist/sexist diatribes against me, which were being praised by my peers. I’m told you can’t be racist against white men. What, they can’t take it? In the years 2019-2021 no white men appear in the best novel short lists at all (in 2022 Andy Weir breaks this with Project Hail Mary. That is the level of success needed to be considered for a Hugo then.)

I realize I haven’t enjoyed most of what I’ve been reading for years.

The final blow comes in 2020. It’s the second year of the awards lockout. “A Memory Called Empire” wins the Hugo. When I first reviewed it I said

> “there is nothing exceptional about this. It’s…. fine. It’s fine. But it’s not good . It’s certainly not genre-defining or among the best things published that year. […]I know there’s at least one Hugo nominated novel that I just don’t get every year, but I don’t think anyone is doing Martine a favor by pretending they think her novel is a Hugo contender. I feel bad that this happened.”

Upon its winning I wrote

> I can no longer say anything is “Hugo material” or not, because my judgements of quality do not mesh with the audience of the Hugos. […] I gotta go looking for a community that is more like me

# Advancing the frontier of cryptanalysis

Today, we’re sharing new research from @GoogleDeepMind showing how AI agents can accelerate cryptanalysis, or the science of stress-testing encryption. Our team used AI agents, guided by human supervision, to uncover two major weaknesses on legacy 1024-bit RSA-based cryptosystems, showing that these systems can be compromised with a lower computational budget than previously thought possible.

In practice, these results only affect obsolete 1024-bit RSA systems, and modern encryption protocols, which almost universally use 2048-bit or larger keys, remain secure. They do, however, show how rapidly AI agent systems can evaluate the mathematical "hardness" of the computational problems that underpin digital security. We are sharing this research so that the security community can use these insights to better measure cryptographic strength, and keep modern standards resilient well ahead of potential threats.

From encrypted communications to digital currencies, modern encryption systems rely on the concept of computational "hardness": mathematical problems that are easy to set up but computationally infeasible for attackers to solve. For decades, systems like RSA have relied on this fact — multiplying two large prime numbers together is easy, but reversing that process (factorising their product) is computationally much harder.

At the same time, the cryptanalysis community has continuously stress-tested and questioned these hardness assumptions to ensure security standards stay ahead of potential threats, using retired systems like RSA-1024 as safe proving grounds, as we did here.

Historically, major advances in this kind of work take years or decades, meaning defenders could assume hardness margins changed only slowly. Our results, led by Dj Dvijotham and Abhradeep Thakurta and in collaboration with Nadia Heninger (UC San Diego and Inria), Emmanuel Thomé (Inria), show that AI can probe these hardness assumptions much faster, making proactive stress-testing more important than ever.

Our first result is about cryptanalysis and has consequences for the security of digital signatures. This is how computers verify that a piece of data — called a message, such as a software update, document or a website — is genuine and really comes from its claimed source.

Before signing a message, many signature standards add preset data, known as “padding”, to fill it out into a fixed-sized block. Cryptographers knew that padding helps prevent forgery, but not how much protection it offers if an attacker is able to feed chosen inputs to a signing device.

We found a strong answer: what matters is how much of the signed block an attacker controls. Once they control roughly half of the block or more, padding adds no protection at all. Forging a signature becomes just as vulnerable to mathematical shortcuts as using no padding at all. Testing this result in a sandboxed simulation—without touching any live systems—our agents engineered an implementation on an already-solved 1024-bit benchmark key from an earlier academic study, reproducing the result with 3.5× less CPU time, and at less than a thousandth of the computing power needed to break the key itself.

When an attacker controls less of the block, like with a short 32-byte digital fingerprint in the message, forging a signature is harder. Even so, we discovered a new algorithm that, according to our theoretical estimates, improves on the previous best method by roughly 1,600x for 1024-bit keys.

Our second result concerns factorising many numbers of the same size: a key question for RSA because keys typically share standard bit length, such as 1024 or 2048 bits. In theory, an attacker trying to break many keys can spread the cost of one large up-front computation across all of them, lowering the cost per key. Our AI agents discovered a new algorithm with better asymptotic complexity than previously known methods, cutting the average cost of factoring each additional 1024-bit key, out of many, by about 30× compared to previous batch methods.

Together, these results show that in a new era of AI-enabled mathematics and computation, we cannot treat cryptographic hardness as a fixed assumption. Using AI to rigorously test our previously held assumptions will ensure that modern encryption stays secure.

For more details on these results from the Google DeepMind Science team, please read our full technical papers on digital signatures and key factorisation .
